exercises.objective: Compute a Deep Sets aggregation and verify its permutation invariance.
exercises.prompt: Using the Deep Sets formula $f(X)\approx\rho\big(\sum_{x\in X}\phi(x)\big)$ with $\phi(x)=x^2$, $\rho(s)=\sqrt{s}$, and $X=\{1,2,3\}$, compute $f(X)$. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
hints: First apply $\phi$ to each element and sum: $1^2+2^2+3^2$.

$f(X)=\sqrt{14}\approx3.742$. Note the sum is invariant to the order in which you add $1^2,2^2,3^2$, that's exactly why this construction is permutation-invariant regardless of the order neighbors are observed in.

exercises.objective: Explain how a GNN's aggregate step generalizes Deep Sets.
exercises.prompt: Explain how a GNN node's aggregate step, $\text{MLP}_\rho\big(\sum_{m\in N(n)}\text{MLP}_\phi(h_m^{(l)})\big)$, is a direct instance of the Deep Sets formula, and what set is being aggregated over.
hints: Compare term by term: $\text{MLP}_\phi$ plays the role of $\phi$, the sum plays the role of $\sum_{x\in X}$, and $\text{MLP}_\rho$ plays the role of $\rho$.

The set $X$ being aggregated over is node $n$'s neighborhood $N(n)$, a set of neighbor feature vectors $h_m^{(l)}$, not raw sensor readings; it's variable-size and unordered, exactly the setting Deep Sets was designed for.

So a GNN's aggregate step is literally a Deep Sets computation applied locally at every node, once per layer, over that node's (possibly changing) set of neighbors; the update step then combines this aggregated summary with the node's own previous feature.

exercises.objective: Explain how a Markov game generalizes RL-01's single-agent MDP.
exercises.prompt: RL-01 defines an MDP as $(S,A,P,R,P_0,\gamma)$. Explain precisely what changes, and what stays the same in form, when generalizing to a Markov game with $N$ robots.
hints: $S$, $P_0$, and $\gamma$ keep the same role and form; $S$ becomes the *joint* state space (the combined state of all $N$ robots) rather than one robot's state.

$A$ becomes the joint action space $A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_N$: at every step, all $N$ robots choose an action simultaneously, and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ depends on the whole joint action, not any single robot's action alone.

$R$ splits into $N$ (possibly distinct) reward functions $r_1,\ldots,r_N$, one per robot; whether these coincide (fully cooperative) or sum to zero (competitive) determines the game's reward structure, a distinction that doesn't exist in the single-agent MDP at all.

exercises.objective: Explain why MARL's non-stationarity challenge doesn't arise in single-agent RL.
exercises.prompt: From a single robot's own point of view, training alongside other learning robots whose policies aren't directly observable, explain why the environment can appear non-Markovian even though the true underlying Markov game is stationary.
hints: The true joint transition function $P(s'\mid s,a)$ (over the joint state and joint action) is fixed and Markovian; that's not what's breaking.

But a single robot only observes its own state/action/reward, not the other robots' policies; from its narrow point of view, the same observed state can lead to different outcomes at different times, purely because the *other* robots' policies are changing (they're learning too), not because the world itself is changing.

So 'the same state leading to different outcomes over time' looks exactly like a non-Markovian environment from that single robot's restricted viewpoint, even though the full joint system is a perfectly well-defined, stationary Markov game; this is why independent learners in MARL are especially hard to get to converge.
